reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents an instructional demonstration and promotion of DoorDash referral credits, including signup conditions and a checkout showing credits applied to an order. The requested actions are signing up through a referral link and inviting others, presented as ordinary conditions for receiving platform credits. Although the video uses strong “100%” wording and encourages broad sharing, the available video evidence does not establish that the offer was fraudulent or caused a harmful outcome.

If you sign up using that link, you'll get $7 credit.
You'll literally get 15 and then you'll get 7 if you invite other people and That credit just keeps on adding up.
you can literally see even with the tip itself credits applied $26 $0 I literally paid or if I ordered will pay zero dollars.
you can go join Facebook groups and like I said, you can share everywhere and ask people to just sign up for it.

opening.argument: The central promise is free food or unusually easy account credit, but obtaining it is tied to specific actions: using the supplied signup link and recruiting other people. The description says the method works every time and directs viewers to use its link, while the speaker explains that signup and invitations generate credits. This is not merely discussion of DoorDash; it is a reward solicitation built around participation and referral activity. The checkout screen reinforces the promised outcome by showing a $26 order reduced to $0 through applied credits. The reward therefore depends on a viewer entering the platform through the promoted pathway and, for accumulating credit, inducing others to do the same.

You'll literally get 15 and then you'll get 7 if you invite other people
credits applied $26 $0 I literally paid or if I ordered will pay zero dollars.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an ordinary promotion does not remove the core promise-action structure. The cited signup and invitation conditions are precisely what make the reward contingent on viewer participation, while the checkout example is presented as proof that the promised free-food result works. The defense also acknowledges encouragement to share links broadly, which makes the solicitation central rather than incidental.

citations.quote: You'll literally get 15 and then you'll get 7 if you invite other people
you can share everywhere and ask people to just sign up for it.
This is not fake. This is legit guys.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These quotes show a referral reward, not a deceptive reward scheme. The speaker identifies signup and invitations as conditions, and the checkout screen shows credits applied, but neither establishes that the credits were unavailable, fabricated, or harmful. A contingent promotional benefit can be a legitimate platform incentive even when participation is requested.

opening.argument: Several genuine warning signals appear together: an absolute success claim, urgency, an external signup link, and a large-looking reward relative to the required effort. The title promises free food and says it is “100% Working,” the description says “Act now,” and the speaker promotes $15 and $7 credits that increase when additional people are invited. The referral screen visibly connects those amounts to sharing a link and a referred person's first order. The presentation also encourages posting referral links across Reddit, Facebook groups, and comments. Individually these could be ordinary marketing features, but together they create a low-barrier reward pitch that pressures viewers to act before carefully checking eligibility, limits, or fulfillment.

citations.quote: How To Get Free Food From DoorDash 2020!! 100% Working!
Act now! Get $15 off ($5 off each of your first 3 orders) when you sign up with this link:
You'll literally get 15 and then you'll get 7 if you invite other people
you can go join Facebook groups and like I said, you can share everywhere and ask people to just sign up for it.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the presence of platform mechanics as reassurance, but it does not answer the unusually confident framing. “100%” and “Act now” are not neutral descriptions, and the invitation to distribute referral links everywhere turns the audience into a recruitment channel. Showing a credit balance or a discounted checkout does not establish that every viewer will qualify or receive the advertised result.

citations.quote: 100% Working!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warning signals are marketing language, not proof of deception. The offer is described with concrete conditions: signup, referral, and a first order, while the screen shows a stated credit program rather than an invented investment or payment demand. The evidence does not show that the urgency caused a loss, that eligibility was concealed, or that the credits failed.

citations.quote: Get $15 off ($5 off each of your first 3 orders) when you sign up with this link:
some of the links above are affiliate links

opening.argument: Although styled as a step-by-step tutorial, the video functions as a direct promotion for the creator's referral pathway. It repeatedly directs viewers to the description and comments, recommends using the creator's link, invites viewers to recruit friends, and even welcomes more referral links in the comments. The instructional framing therefore serves the solicitation: viewers are encouraged to sign up, spread links, and generate credits, while the creator benefits from referral activity. The description's affiliate disclosure further confirms that the surrounding links are monetized promotional material. The claimed educational role does not change the fact that the video's practical endpoint is audience participation in a reward funnel.

citations.quote: I want to basically show you what you need to do and basically step by step guide
If you sign up using that link, you'll get $7 credit.
if you want to leave your referral link in the description below in the comments section below more than happy to do so
some of the links above are affiliate links

rebuttal.rebuttal: The tutorial label is not decisive when the speaker's practical instructions repeatedly steer viewers to referral links and further recruitment. The defense's description of ordinary conditions actually confirms that participation is the video's intended endpoint. A disclaimer about commissions does not cure the aggressive promotion or establish that the promised benefit is reliably available to viewers.

citations.quote: If you sign up using that link, you'll get $7 credit.
you can share everywhere and ask people to just sign up for it.
I will earn a commission if you decide to make a purchase after clicking through the link.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The evidence supports transparent promotion, not a disguised scheme. The description expressly discloses affiliate commissions, and the speaker explains the referral conditions instead of asking viewers for deposits, sensitive verification, or investment funds. The tutorial may encourage participation, but the supplied material does not show that the platform reward is fraudulent or that viewers suffer a harmful outcome.
